corrections.original: All src/runtime execution is JS on the CPU ... only JSON search runs on WebGPU.
corrections.fix: Scope to the shipped demos: of the three src/ demos only src/json-search runs on WebGPU (the doc says 'e.g.'). Many lab experiments also run on WebGPU (lab/knuth-plass/gpu, lab/json-search/gpu, lab/ui-exploration/codegen, pixel-output, instanced-items, text-walker, event-time, user-population).

corrections.original: A settle check is the only evaluation where a moving spring (within 0.01 px and 0.01 px/s) lands and stops.
corrections.fix: Add the repo's own exception: 'The one exception is a snap, which pins the thumb onto its destination when a frame would need more than 300 steps'.

corrections.original: Every stored table and drawn output at a shared timestamp is bit-identical at every frame rate (with 'events and settle checks').
corrections.fix: It is a measured result 'in the same traces' of spring-matrix.test.ts (10/30/60/120 fps, 500 ms stalls). It holds 'as long as no snap runs' and while events arrive in timestamp order. Say 'in the repo's tests', not 'always'.

corrections.original: Fiedler 2004 names the 'spiral of death' and describes the accumulator that carries leftover time; the familiar belief is to carry the backlog, capped.
corrections.fix: Fiedler writes 'the so called "spiral of death"', so he did not coin it. His accumulator carries only the remainder below one dt, and his loop clamps frameTime to 0.25 s ('if ( frameTime > 0.25 ) frameTime = 0.25;'), so a long backlog is dropped. That is closer to discard than to ui.md's carry. The date Jun 10, 2004 is confirmed.

corrections.original: The cap of 300 steps is 75 times the 4 steps a normal 60 fps frame needs.
corrections.fix: About 72 times: 16.67 ms / 4 ms = 4.17 steps per 60 fps frame, and 300 / 4.17 = 72. Quote the doc instead: '300 steps against about 4 per frame at 60 fps'.

corrections.original: The toggle's press -> armed -> release -> flip works over two separate evaluations.
corrections.fix: That holds only when the press and release have distinct timestamps. Events that share a timestamp apply in one evaluation in the fixed order down, then up, then cancel (armedAfterDown), so the switch can arm and flip in one evaluation.

corrections.original: Scenario C: simulated time always lands on exact 64 ms multiples, whatever the frame rate.
corrections.fix: Only committed settle-check times land on clock start + 64k ms (absent events). Frame previews are simulated to the frame time on the 4 ms step grid (e.g. 100 ms at 10 fps).

corrections.original: Event handlers only queue timestamped events.
corrections.fix: The quote is verbatim and correct in meaning: handlers don't evaluate or write state. But in the code each pointer handler also calls scheduleRender() to request a frame, and so does the resize listener. Don't animate handlers as doing nothing but enqueueing.

corrections.original: Quote 11 note: the line break falls after 'evaluations. It'.
corrections.fix: In host-timing.ts the comment's line 3 ends with 'It never' and line 4 begins 'builds operations'. The quote text itself is verbatim once the // markers are removed.

corrections.original: About 5% of frames drew a different column count.
corrections.fix: 'about 5% of frames at 60 fps drew a different column count'.

corrections.original: Timeline: springs stored absolute positions until 2026-09-14; 'Measured afterwards' ...
corrections.fix: Removed 'Measured afterwards'. The source only says the absolute-position form lasted 'until September 14, 2026' and that the text was moved into status.md on October 15, 2026. When the measurement was taken is not stated.
2026-10-16 17:33:49 -0700 is 2026-10-17T00:33:49Z in UTC (GitHub API). As of 2026-10-27 it is still the head of main (825 commits, 2,034 stars, MIT, public).
